doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Manhattan School of Music and Eddie Durham
title: Warmth of older Black musicians and music as life
summary: Being welcomed as a young Jewish kid by older Black musicians; music comes out of life; link to teaching context.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: that’s a dangerous thing to do, to generalize. All I can talk about is the people that I was with. And I experienced things and the music, and that’s I mean I didn’t realize it then. I’m just starting to realize it now. But the music was all part of that. The music is not just something — I’ve just come to realize this recently at sixty, but you know the music is not just something that happens on the bandstand with C7 and A7 and an old Lester Young solo. You know. The music is something that comes out of the life and out of the experience and out of all these things. Boy do I wish I had learned that lesson a lot earlier in life. But now I can look back and see all that, and how I was the beneficiary of that, and that kind of — no pun intended — colored my way of understanding things. So that was a tremendously significant thing while I was in college.

Well that explains I think partly one of your answers early on today with the sociology and the musicology. And I can also see why you spend so much preparation time with your jazz history class, not to just start out with a person, okay here we go, Louis Armstrong and move forward.
